analysis.one_liner: Requires 401(k) plans to disclose all fees to workers and employers, with penalties for hiding them.
analysis.headline: A House subcommittee approved the bill 13–8 in June 2009, but the full Education and Labor Committee never took it up and it died without a floor vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would force companies that run 401(k) plans and sell the investments inside them to tell employers exactly what they charge, broken into categories like recordkeeping and investment management. Workers would get yearly notices with a plain fee comparison chart for every investment option, and quarterly statements showing the dollars deducted from their accounts. Every plan would have to offer at least one low-cost index fund, and regulators could fine providers up to $1,000 a day per worker for hiding fees.
analysis.who_benefits: The tens of millions of Americans with 401(k) accounts. Hidden fees on 401(k) plans were typically 1–2% of assets a year, which compounds into a large share of a lifetime's savings; the bill would have let workers and their employers see and compare those charges for the first time, and given the Labor Department tools to audit plans and name providers that block compliance [S2][S3].

how_it_helps.text: Employers could not sign any service contract over $5,000 a year unless the provider first delivered a written statement of expected total annual charges, broken out among recordkeeping, transaction, and investment management costs, plus disclosure of conflicts like selling its own funds or free services paid for through participant charges [S2][S3].
Workers would receive, every year, a notice and fee comparison chart for each investment option showing charges in dollars and a history of returns net of fees [S2][S3].
Quarterly statements would itemize the actual charges deducted from each participant's account during the quarter [S3].

Every plan offering participant-directed investing would have to include at least one passively managed index fund matching the whole U.S. stock or bond market, with no government or employer endorsement [S2][S3].

Providers that hid required fees could face civil penalties up to $1,000 per participant per day, capped at 10% of the amount involved, and the Labor Department would have to report providers with a pattern of blocking compliance to regulators and widely disclose their identity [S2][S3].
The Labor Department would annually audit a representative sample of plans for compliance and give small employers help finding low-cost options [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: 401(k) service providers — recordkeepers, plan administrators, and investment firms — would bear the cost of itemizing and disclosing their compensation, plus penalties for nondisclosure. Employers sponsoring plans would face new notice and statement duties, softened for small plans by annual-instead-of-quarterly statements, an electronic delivery option, and Labor Department compliance help [S2][S3].

drawbacks.text: The disclosure and quarterly-statement requirements add compliance work for every employer offering a 401(k), and the bill provides civil penalties of up to $100 a day for failing to deliver the required participant notices, which small businesses could find burdensome even with the bill's small-plan accommodations and Labor Department assistance [S3].

The bill requires plans to include one index fund but does not force anyone to use it, so workers who never read the disclosures would still pay high fees; the remedy depends on employers shopping providers, and disclosure alone does not cap what any provider may charge [S2][S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit side is large and durable: fees charged quietly every year compound over a career, so even modest disclosure-driven fee shopping is worth a substantial share of workers' retirement savings. The cost side is real but narrower — paperwork for employers and reduced fee income and pricing flexibility for the financial industry. An honest supporter would acknowledge that disclosure is an indirect tool; it pressures prices down over time rather than setting them directly.

outcome.mechanism: A House subcommittee approved it 13–8 in June 2009 and sent it to the full Education and Labor Committee, but the full committee never marked it up and it never reached the House floor before the Congress ended [S5][S1].

narrative.text: The bill was introduced April 21, 2009 by Rep. George Miller of California with ten Democratic cosponsors, and referred to the House Committee on Education and Labor [S1][S4][S5].
On May 21, 2009 it went to the Subcommittee on Health, Employment, Labor, and Pensions, which held a mark-up on June 17 and forwarded an amended bill to the full committee by a 13–8 vote [S5].
The full Education and Labor Committee took no further action, and the bill died there when the 111th Congress ended in January 2011 [S5][S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: 401(k) recordkeeping and investment firms kept collecting fees without standardized advance disclosure to employers or workers, and kept fees and conflicts of interest out of participants' quarterly statements. Employers were spared the compliance work. Notably, the sponsor chaired the full committee that never took the bill up, so the outcome also spared employers and providers the compliance costs the bill would have imposed.

industries.note: These firms would have to itemize and disclose in advance all compensation tied to a plan contract, including payments hidden inside fund share classes and 'free' services recouped from participant accounts, with penalties up to $1,000 per participant per day for hiding fees. Their business model depended on charges participants could not easily see or compare.

The bill would force disclosure of why in-plan share prices differ from retail prices and whether a provider profits from selling its own funds, and would require every plan to carry a low-cost index fund option. Both measures would pressure the high-fee, actively managed funds that pay for distribution in 401(k) plans.

Small employers would face new disclosure and notice duties and penalty exposure, but plans with 100 or fewer participants could file statements annually instead of quarterly, disclosures could be electronic, and the bill directs the Labor Department to give small employers help comparing providers and fees.
